h: פָּרָשַׁת פָּרָה, מַאֲמָר ז׳ Parshas Parah — Maamar Zayin

p: From the haftarah of Parshas Parah,
which does not speak at all
but only of purification from sins and transgressions,
"And I will sprinkle upon you," etc.,
"and from all your idols I will purify you,
and I will give you a new heart," etc.,
וְעָשִׂיתִי אֵת אֲשֶׁר בְּחֻקַּי תֵּלֵכוּ וְגוֹמֵר
"and I will bring it about that you walk in My statutes," etc.,
what is the connection of this haftarah
From this it is clear, as we said,
that the main purification of the parah
is from the root of the yetzer hara,
and it purifies from all impurity,
even from the impurity of the dead,
which the serpent brought into the world.
which stems from hatred of people
and the kelipah of anger and jealousy,
and it is the kelipah of Esav.
which is strange cravings and loves.
And the impurity of the dead
corresponds to the kelipah of pride and honor,
and it is the root of the serpent's enticement:
branch out the three severe sins:
עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה גִּלּוּי עֲרָיוֹת וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים
For the ultimate end of pride is
עַד שֶׁאָמַר אֶעֱלֶה עַל בָּמֳתֵי עָב
to the point that he said, "I will ascend above the heights of the clouds,
I will be like the Most High."
And we also find the impurity of neveilah and sheretz,
which is not in a person's own body.
that they compared one who has a sin in his hand
and confesses but does not turn back from it
to a person holding a sheretz in his hand,
who, even if he immerses, etc.,
his immersion does not take effect.
And this is because in truth all the impurities
הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי קִלְקוּל הַנָּחָשׁ
come only through the corruption of the serpent,
who put desire and the yetzer hara into man;
from this impurity is found in animals,
such as sheratzim and the like.
And therefore they cited the impurity of a sheretz:
though it is an impurity of a living creature,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּל זְמַן שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְתַקֵּן הַחֵטְא
nevertheless, as long as he does not rectify the sin,
the purification and immersion do not take effect.
וְעַל יְדֵי טָהֳרַת הַלֵּב מֵהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע
And through purifying the heart from the yetzer hara,
as will be in the future,
"And I will remove the heart of stone
עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִתְבַּטֵּל כָּל הַטּוּמְאוֹת
through this all the impurities will be nullified
הַבָּאִים עַל יְדֵי יֵצֶר הָרָע וְהַקְּלִיפּוֹת
that come through the yetzer hara and the kelipos,
And this is what it says (ibid. 25),
"And you will be purified from all your impurities,
and from all your idols," etc.
And likewise the purification of the parah indicates
from the entire root of the serpent's corruption,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵשׁ טָהֳרָה לְכָל הַטּוּמְאוֹת
and through this there is purification for all the impurities,
even for the impurity of the dead,
for which one is not sent out even from the Levite camp,
because this kelipah applies even to great people
And corresponding to this impurity is the kelipah of Amalek,
"'A man's pride will bring him low' (Mishlei 29:23) —
And it is the first of the kelipah.
"And I will give you a new heart," etc.,
"and My spirit I will put within you," etc.,
"And I will save you from all your impurities," etc. —
And this is that at the coming of Mashiach,
who will be an individual who did teshuvah,
for whose sake the whole world is forgiven
thoughts of teshuvah into the heart of all Yisrael,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם יִהְיוּ הָאוֹבְדִים בְּאֶרֶץ אַשּׁוּר
still there will be "those lost in the land of Ashur,"
and they do not know at all
וְעִם כָּל זֶה עַל יְדֵי הַשּׁוֹפָר גָּדוֹל
and even so, through the great shofar
meaning that Hashem Yisbarach, from His side,
from the aspect of the higher teshuvah,
which is Binah, the great shofar,
and "no outcast shall be cast away from Him" —
anyone who is of the seed of Yisrael.
"And I will save you from all your impurities."
וְהִנֵּה שַׁבָּת אִיתָא (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב רד, א)
Now, regarding Shabbos it is stated (Zohar II 204a):
the shin is the secret of the three Avos,
and the bas, the daughter, is crowned with them" —
the holiness of the three Avos.
that the holiness of the Avos serves
to nullify the three kelipos and impurities.
For Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him,
And Yitzchak counters the kelipah of desire,
one is saved from all desires.
And Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
counters the kelipah of pride and honor,
for he was lowly in his own eyes
And then, when they merit the holiness of the Avos,
they merit to be purified from all the kelipos
And this is what they said in the Pesikta for Parah
כֵּיצַד יֵשׁ בָּהּ שֶׁבַע פָּרוֹת כּוּלֵּי
How so? It contains seven cows," etc.,
when they were about to burn," etc.,
"they sprinkle upon him all seven days,
And the intent is that each day they would sprinkle
from all the chataos that were there,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפָרָה (פֶּרֶק ג מִשְׁנָה א)
that is, from all the chataos
made since the days of Moshe,
And the Pesikta is a proof for this explanation,
for according to the Bartenura's explanation,
that each day they would sprinkle
from the ash of a different cow,
לֹא הָיוּ כָּאן אַרְבָּעִים וְתֵשַׁע הַזָּיוֹת
there would not be forty-nine sprinklings here.
שֶׁהָיוּ מַזִּין בְּכָל יוֹם מִכָּל הַחַטָּאוֹת
they sprinkled each day from all the chataos;
and we learned (ibid.), "If they did not find from seven," etc.,
that ideally they needed from seven,
And as for what the Tosfos Yom Tov wrote
as proof for the Bartenura's explanation,
מִמַּה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ לֹא מָצְאוּ מִשֶּׁבַע וְכוּ׳
from what they said, "If they did not find from seven," etc. —
"for from where would we know that seven are needed,
on the contrary, from there is a compelling proof to the opposite,
for according to the Bartenura and the Rambam
it would be difficult: on Shabbos
and if so, they would never need
But according to what we wrote,
and it was known that "all the chataos"
means the seven made since the days of Moshe,
וְעַל זֶה תְּנַן לֹא מָצְאוּ מִשֶּׁבַע כּוּלֵּי
regarding this we learned, "If they did not find from seven," etc. —
וְכֵן פֵּירֵשׁ הַגְּאוֹן רַבִּי אֵלִיָּהוּ זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה
And so the Gra, of blessed memory, explained
and he emends the text to "from all seven chataos";
אַךְ עַל כָּל פָּנִים יֵשׁ לְהָבִין
But in any case we must understand
what they said in the Pesikta,
since they set him apart on the fourth day of the week
כִּי הֵיכִי דְּנִתְרְמֵי רְבִיעִי שֶׁלּוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת
so that his fourth day would fall on Shabbos,
as they said in the Gemara (ibid.).
And according to what we said,
like the power of the parah's sprinklings,
for on Shabbos she is crowned with the Avos,
and we merit the holiness of the Avos,
and it is as if the sprinklings were done
on Shabbos too, as mentioned above.
And this is why it counted forty-nine sprinklings,
together with the power of Shabbos,
שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ הַשֶּׁבַע הַזָּיוֹת
which is also like the seven sprinklings;
which corresponds to Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him
[פְּרִי עֵץ חַיִּים שַׁעַר הַשַּׁבָּת פֶּרֶק יח]
when the Jew merits his holiness —
for he was lowly in his own eyes, as mentioned above —
we say (in the zemer Bnei Heichala),
for the kelipah of Amalek is a dog,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב סה, א)
and it corresponds to the impurity of the dead,
which is from the kelipah of pride, as mentioned above.
And it is like the purification of the parah,
which purifies even from the impurity of the dead.
And so we read the parshah of Parah on Shabbos,
for it is all one, as stated.

paragraphs.text: Yechezkel 36:25–29, haftarah for Parah — “I shall sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall become pure. From all your impurities and all your idols I shall purify you. I shall give you a new heart and place a new spirit within you; I shall remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I shall place My spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, to keep My judgments and perform them. ... I shall save you from all your impurities.” The haftarah explicitly moves from water and impurity to the renewal of the heart and conduct. This is the basis of Rav Tzadok's reading of Parah as purification from the root of sin.

paragraphs.text: Taanit 16a — “Rav Adda bar Ahavah said: One who has a transgression in his hand, confesses, and does not turn away from it is like a person holding a creeping creature in his hand. Even if he immerses in all the waters of the world, his immersion does not avail. If he throws it from his hand, as soon as he immerses in forty seah, his immersion avails, as it is said, One who confesses and abandons will receive mercy.” Confession must accompany abandonment of the sin. Rav Tzadok draws from the image that inner repentance is the root of purification.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b — “Rabbi Meir would say: Great is repentance, for on account of one individual who repents the whole world is forgiven, as it is said, I shall heal their backsliding; I shall love them freely, for My anger has turned away from him. It does not say from them, but from him.” The identification of that individual with Mashiach, who awakens repentance in all Israel, is Rav Tzadok's development of this teaching.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 5 — “Mashiach is the individual who did teshuvah, for whose sake the world is forgiven: he will put a thought of teshuvah into the whole. For surely they will not forgive the whole world for nothing.” This explains why the forgiveness is not arbitrary. Mashiach ben Yosef purifies those who never fell. Mashiach ben David brings teshuvah into the hearts of those who did.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shemos 10 — “Just as Moshe had to be raised in Pharaoh’s house… so Mashiach, who must bring out even those lost in Ashur though they are sunk deep, must dwell with them in the land.” This adds how even the fully assimilated are reached. The redeemer stands among them, as Moshe did in Egypt, and their kelipah does not touch him.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shemos 8 — “The great shofar is Binah (Zohar III 266b): when fear enters the point in the heart, the awakening in the depths of the heart helps even those cast away… and even those lost in Ashur.” This explains how Binah reaches those who do not know they are Jews. The awakening comes from beneath awareness, at the point of the heart, and not through their own understanding.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayera 1 — “These three kelipos stand against the three Avos in holiness: Avraham brings all loves into holiness, Yitzchak the strengths… and honor stands against Yaakov the small, as it says, ‘I am too small.’” Rav Tzadok there also ties the three to Avos 2:11 (evil eye, yetzer hara, hatred of people) and to Bilaam’s traits. He shows why lowliness frees one from desire as well.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbasi 14:6, Parah — “This section too is refined sevenfold: it contains forty-nine purifications. How? Seven cows, seven burnings, seven sprinklings, seven priests, seven impure ones, seven pure ones, and seven washings. Moreover, when they wished to burn the sin-offering cow, they sprinkled upon its priest all seven days, seven sprinklings each day: thus forty-nine sprinklings, refined sevenfold.” Rav Tzadok compares this forty-ninefold statement with the Mishnah and Yoma's practical rule excluding Shabbos sprinkling. His final resolution assigns Shabbos an inward purifying force.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Parah 3:1 — “Seven days before the heifer is burned, the priest who will burn it is separated from his home to the chamber northeast of the Temple court, called the Stone House. They sprinkle upon him all seven days from all the purification offerings that were there. Rabbi Yosei says: They sprinkled only on the third and seventh. Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests, says: Upon the priest who burns the heifer they sprinkle all seven days; upon the Yom Kippur priest, only on the third and seventh.” The phrase from all the purification offerings is the subject of the differing interpretations that follow.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Parah 3:5 — “If they did not find ashes from seven, they prepared from six, five, four, three, two, or one. Who prepared them? Moshe prepared the first and Ezra the second; five were prepared from Ezra onward, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say: Seven were prepared from Ezra onward.” Rabbi Meir's five after Ezra, together with Moshe's and Ezra's, give seven in total. The Sages' count gives nine; Rav Tzadok follows Rabbi Meir in explaining the sevenfold sprinkling.

paragraphs.text: Bartenura, Parah 3:1 — “From all the purification offerings that were there: from all the cows prepared from Moshe our teacher's days until that time, for a little from each cow was set aside as a reserve. On the first day they sprinkled upon him from one cow's ashes, on the second from another, and on the third from another.” Bartenura assigns a different cow's ashes to each day. Rav Tzadok argues instead for sprinkling from every available cow each day.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos Yom Tov, Parah 3:1, s.v. Mikol — “Bartenura explains: On the first day they sprinkle from one cow's ashes, on the second from another. So Rambam wrote in his commentary: each day he should be sprinkled with ashes other than those used on any preceding day. What compels this explanation, it appears to me, is the later Mishnah, If they did not find from seven. If every day they sprinkled from all that were there, why mention seven? ... Rather, each day means from one purification offering.” Rav Tzadok disputes this proof. The source's reasoning is quoted before his counterargument, rather than rewritten to agree with him.

paragraphs.text: Gra, Eliyahu Rabbah, Parah 3:1 — “We read: From all seven purification offerings that were there. ... The anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who says five were prepared after Ezra; under the Sages' view there would be nine. Sprinkling from all seven is an added safeguard: perhaps one cow had been prepared more correctly than another. Each day they sprinkled from all seven for that reason, so that throughout all seven days he would receive sprinkling from the more correctly prepared one.” This explicitly supports Rav Tzadok's reading, including the textual addition seven and the use of all seven every day.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 8b — “Rava said: The High Priest for Yom Kippur, whose date depends on the calendar rather than our choice, must be separated on the third of Tishrei, whatever day it falls. But the priest who burns the heifer, whose timing is in our hands, is separated on Wednesday so that his fourth day will fall on Shabbos.” The preceding discussion excludes Shabbos sprinkling. Rav Tzadok therefore asks how the Midrash counts forty-nine actual sprinklings, then explains Shabbos's inward contribution.

paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaShabbos 18, third meal — “Although judgment awakens at Minchah on the other weekdays, ... now, at Shabbos Minchah, all is simple mercy: supreme kindness is revealed in the brow of Arich Anpin, and when He looks below, all judgments are subdued. ... This meal is attached to the verse I shall feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father. ... At the third meal judgments are not mentioned at all; all is complete mercy. Therefore Moshe departed at this hour rather than in the morning, to signify that he was concealed within simple mercy.” The passage explains Shabbos Minchah as mercy prevailing at the time normally associated with judgment. Rav Tzadok applies that state to the inward purification supplied by Shabbos.

p: It is known that the holiness of Shabbos
shines forth to sanctify the weekdays
with a semblance of the holiness of that Shabbos.
And since the Shabbos was Parshas Parah,
and they said in the Yerushalmi
[מְגִילָּה פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ה כה, ב]
that we do not interrupt between it and Parshas HaChodesh
and it is explained in the Pesikta
that the purification of the parah is refined sevenfold —
seven cows and seven sprinklings, etc. —
of all seven sefiros of holiness,
certainly they are purified in the weekdays
until Shabbos Kodesh of Parshas HaChodesh,
when they enter the ultimate holiness in completeness.
Now, the first of the attributes in holiness
פְּסוֹלֶת שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
the dross of Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him,
who is the kindness and love of holiness.
And the main surge of desire
is in the days of youth;
he will merit the aspect of "the kindness of your youth,"
which is the very beginning of holiness,
these are the young men of Yisrael
who have not tasted the taste of sin."
And this was the root of the soul
of Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him:
the aspect of love of kindness.
And as we heard from our holy Rebbe,
זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה לְחַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
of blessed and holy memory, for the life of the World to Come,
הַפֵּירוּשׁ עַל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת פט, ב)
the explanation of what they said (Shabbos 89b):
"Neither is there sense in the elders,
nor counsel in the young children" —
שֶׁסָּבָא הוּא יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
the elder is Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
and in whom the aspect of holiness had become threefold.
קָאֵי עַל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
refers to Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him,
who was the beginning of holiness,
as in the days of youth.
And by overcoming, in these days,
one merits the threefold love of holiness:
love of the Torah, and love of Yisrael,
the Holy One, blessed be He, the Torah, and Yisrael.
And likewise, these are found in Avraham Avinu,
that the Holy One, blessed be He, provided him
with his two kidneys like two teachers,
וְהָיוּ נוֹבְעוֹת וּמְלַמְּדוֹת אוֹתוֹ תּוֹרָה כּוּלֵּי
which would well forth and teach him Torah, etc.
for he would take in guests
and bring them close to Hashem Yisbarach, as is known.
Now, as we heard from our holy Rebbe,
זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה לְחַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
of blessed and holy memory, for the life of the World to Come,
דְּעִנְיַן טוּמְאַת מֵת הוּא מִדַּת הָעַצְבוּת
the matter of impurity of the dead is the trait of sadness,
which is the camp of the Shechinah;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מְרַמֵּז טָהֳרַת פָּרָה
and to this the purification of the parah alludes:
to be purified from the aspect of sadness,
וְגַם אִם הוּא מֵאוֹתוֹ עִנְיָן עַצְמוֹ
And even if it comes from that very matter —
that he feels he is not clean of desire
and the yetzer hara overpowers him in this —
עִם כָּל זֶה לֹא יַרְפֶּה אֶת עַצְמוֹ
nevertheless he should not let himself go slack,
It is like what they said (Sukkah 52a):
that he could not restrain himself,
until a certain elder taught him —
his inclination is greater than his."
For on the contrary, the more a person enters
and "Hashem will not leave him in his hand,"
for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not
make unreasonable demands of His creatures
וְהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁל כָּל אֶחָד בִּפְרָט
and the yetzer hara of each individual
was not implanted in him beyond his strength,
רַק כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁיּוּכַל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו
but only as much as he can overcome.
when he strengthens himself and prevails
so as not to fall into sadness —
And this is the matter of the purification of Parshas Parah,
"Who can bring purity out of impurity?" —
שֶׁכָּל הָעוֹסְקִין בְּפָרָה מִתְּחִילָּה וְעַד סוֹף
for all who are involved with the parah from beginning to end
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה חֻקַּת יט, א).
(as is written in Midrash Rabbah Chukas 19:1).
And this belongs to the category of things
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁעַל זֶה מְרַמֵּז הַפָּסוּק
And one may say that the verse alludes to this:
[דְּבָרִים ל, יא] כִּי הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת וְגוֹמֵר
that he is being pushed away
רַק כִּי קָרוֹב אֵלֶיךָ הַדָּבָר מְאֹד
rather, "the matter is very near to you,
in your mouth and in your heart, to do it" —
meaning it is near to you
in the three things mentioned above.
"In your mouth" — that is, in words of Torah,
שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [יְשַׁעְיָה נט, כא] לֹא יָמוּשׁוּ מִפִּיךָ.
as it says (Yeshayah 59:21), "it shall not depart from your mouth."
which is the service of the heart

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 89b — “In the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will tell Avraham: Your children have sinned against Me. He will answer: Master of the world, let them be erased for the sanctity of Your Name. He will say: Let Me tell Yaakov, who endured the pain of raising children; perhaps he will ask mercy for them. He too answers: Let them be erased for the sanctity of Your Name. He says: There is no reason in the elders and no counsel in the children. He tells Yitzchak: Your children have sinned against Me. Yitzchak answers: My children, and not Your children? When they put We shall do before We shall hear, You called them My firstborn son; now they are my children, not Yours?” The Gemara presents Avraham, Yaakov, and Yitzchak in that sequence. The identification of Yaakov with the elder and Avraham with childhood is the teaching of Rav Tzadok's master reported in the discourse.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tzidkas HaTzaddik 202 — “In youth passion and love surge in a person, and then is the time to use love… and measure for measure Hashem loves a person in youth: ‘When Yisrael was a youth, I loved him.’” There Rav Tzadok gives the order of a life: love in youth, then fear with Torah, then settled da’as in old age. It follows the three Avos, with Avraham as the beginning.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sod Yesharim (Radzin), Parshas Parah 8 — “The main impurity is this despair, by which a person gives up on hope; therefore it says, as counsel, ‘Let them take a parah.’” Rav Tzadok heard from his rebbe that corpse-impurity is sadness. The Izhbitzer’s grandson develops the same teaching here. The parah answers despair by revealing a root from which nothing is ever lost.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Chullin 6a, s.v. Ashkechei — “An elder found him: Some explain that wherever the expression that elder appears, it means Eliyahu. But it is impossible to say this in Bameh Madlikin, in the episode of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.” Tosafos reports this identification as some explain and immediately excludes one occurrence. Rav Tzadok applies the identification to the elder who consoles Abaye; it should not be converted into an exceptionless rule.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 3a — “The Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures. Why is the sukkah called an easy commandment? Because it entails no financial loss.” The Gemara discusses giving the nations an opportunity to fulfill the commandment of sukkah. Rav Tzadok applies its general principle to each person's capacity to resist his inclination.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, chapter 27 — “If the sadness is not anxiety about sins but comes from bad thoughts and bad desires that enter his mind, then, when these arise outside the time of divine service, while he is occupied with his affairs and ordinary work, he should, on the contrary, rejoice in his portion, for although these thoughts enter his mind, he turns his attention away from them.... On the contrary, the sadness comes from haughtiness of spirit: he does not recognize his own place, and therefore his heart is troubled that he is not at the level of a tzaddik, to whom such foolish thoughts certainly do not occur.... Therefore a person should not lose heart or be greatly distressed, even if he remains in this battle all his life, for perhaps this is what he was created for, and this is his service: constantly to subdue the other side.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The consolation here concerns the continued presence of temptation, rather than indifference to an actual sin. Tanya identifies the sadness produced by an unrealistic demand to have already become a tzaddik, and treats sustained resistance as a possible lifelong task. This clarifies Rav Tzadok's instruction to persevere when desire is still felt: refusing the additional paralysis of sadness is itself part of the purification, rather than evidence that the original struggle has been ignored.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 19:1 — “Those who work with the heifer from beginning to end render garments impure, while the heifer itself purifies garments. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I have ordained a statute and decreed a decree; you are not permitted to transgress My decree.” The Midrash places the heifer among transformations that defy a simple division between origin and result. Rav Tzadok applies its paradox to persevering in purification despite the painful awareness of impurity.

paragraphs.text: Taanit 2a — “To love Hashem your God and to serve Him with all your heart: What is service that is in the heart? You must say: this is prayer. And afterward it is written, I shall give the rain of your land in its season, the early and late rain.” The Gemara uses this verse to connect rain with prayer. Rav Tzadok draws on its definition of prayer as the work of the heart.
